alignment.note: The Greek opens the clause with καί ('and'); the Peshitta carries the conjunction proclitically on ܘܚܘܘܬܐ ('and serpents'). The Vulgate omits any connective before serpentes, beginning the clause asyndetically, a stylistic Latin preference.

The Greek specifies ἐν ταῖς χερσίν ('in [their] hands') as the explicit means of taking up serpents, but neither the Peshitta nor the Vulgate render this prepositional phrase here; both present simply 'they shall take up serpents,' leaving the instrument implicit.
αἴρω / ܢܫܩܠܘܢ / tollent ('they will take up').
The Vulgate inserts a colon after tollent, segmenting the verse into discrete clauses; neither the Greek nor the Syriac mark this boundary with comparable punctuation in the source tokens.
Greek crasis κἄν ('and if') is unpacked by the Vulgate into et si and rendered by the Peshitta as ܘܐܢ; semantically equivalent conditional connectives.

The Greek single adjective θανάσιμον ('deadly') is matched by Latin mortiferum, but the Syriac uses a noun-genitive construction ܣܡܐ ܕܡܘܬܐ ('poison of death'), making explicit the substance the others leave to context.
Indefinite τι / quid ('anything'), absorbed within the Syriac nominal phrase.

The Greek employs the emphatic double negative οὐ μή ('certainly not') with the future indicative for strong denial; both the Syriac simple ܠܐ and the Latin non render only a single negation, flattening the emphatic Greek construction.
βλάπτω / ܢܗܪ / nocebit ('it will harm'); note Greek 3rd singular vs. Syriac/Latin agreement with the implied poison.
The Vulgate places a second colon after nocebit to close the conditional clause before the next promise; this clause-level punctuation is absent in the Greek and Syriac token streams.

All three attest 'hands' (χεῖρας / ܐܝܕܝܗܘܢ / manus), but the Syriac fronts the noun with a possessive suffix and conjunction ܘܐܝܕܝܗܘܢ ('and their hands') ahead of the prepositional phrase, whereas Greek and Latin place 'hands' after the object of laying-on.
ἐπιτίθημι / ܢܣܝܡܘܢ / imponent ('they will lay on').
Connective καί / et; the Syriac coordination is embedded in the prefixed waw of ܘܢܬܚܠܡܘܢ.

Greek καλῶς ἕξουσιν ('they will be well,' lit. 'have well') and Latin bene habebunt preserve the idiomatic 'have well' construction; the Syriac collapses it into a single reflexive/passive verb ܘܢܬܚܠܡܘܢ ('and they shall be healed'), an idiomatic compression.
